content: Microcephaly, developmental delay, meningoencephalitis, radiolucent bone disease, and jaundice occurring within 24 hours of birth are clinical features that may indicate congenital rubella syndrome (CRS). A laboratory-confirmed CRS case is defined as an infant suspected of having CRS who presents with at least one of the following conditions: cataracts, congenital glaucoma, congenital heart disease, hearing impairment, or pigmentary retinopathy, and meets laboratory criteria for CRS confirmation. Congenital rubella infection (CRI) refers to an infant who does not exhibit the clinical signs of CRS but meets laboratory criteria for CRS. Laboratory confirmation involves nucleic acid detection via RT-PCR or rubella virus isolation from appropriate clinical samples, such as throat swabs (preferred), nasal swabs, blood, urine, or cerebrospinal fluid. Clinical specimens for serology and viral identification should be collected during the initial investigation. Infants with CRI, even without clinical CRS features, typically test positive for rubella-specific IgM at or shortly after birth. However, IgM antibodies may persist for up to one year, and approximately 50% of CRS cases are IgM-negative by six months of age, depending on test sensitivity. If IgM is undetectable in suspected CRS cases shortly after birth, retesting at one month of age or later is recommended. For infants older than six months, laboratory confirmation should not rely solely on IgM testing if results are negative; serial IgG testing should be performed to assess sustained antibody levels over several months. Infants with CRS or CRI should also be tested for rubella virus shedding using virus isolation techniques. Congenitally infected infants may shed and transmit the rubella virus for up to one year, potentially causing outbreaks. This cessation must be confirmed by two negative viral tests conducted one month apart in infants at least three months old. Countries should establish CRS surveillance systems capable of identifying most suspected CRS cases. Routine surveillance should focus on infants under one year of age, although some CRS-associated defects may not become apparent until later in childhood. The most common congenital defects associated with CRS include cataracts, heart defects, and hearing impairment, which are typically identified at secondary and tertiary healthcare facilities. These facilities should serve as sentinel sites for CRS surveillance. To establish CRS surveillance, the following steps are recommended: 1. Identify national CRS surveillance coordinators responsible for epidemiologic and laboratory components. 2. Determine healthcare facilities where CRS cases are likely to be seen and designate them as sentinel surveillance sites. 3. Conduct initial and refresher training for participating sites. 4. Initiate CRS surveillance activities. 5. Assess and monitor surveillance quality. 6. Expand surveillance to additional sites as needed. 7. Analyze CRS surveillance data annually or more frequently if necessary. 8. Provide regular feedback to stakeholders involved in the surveillance system. Rubella in pregnancy registries can be used to follow up on pregnant women exposed to rubella and their pregnancy outcomes, including identifying CRS cases. Retrospective searches of medical records can help establish a baseline for CRS burden in a country, although these cases often lack laboratory confirmation. Retrospective studies can also provide baseline data for evaluating the impact of rubella vaccination programs and documenting CRS elimination. Laboratory surveillance for rubella includes serologic testing and virus detection. Rubella-specific IgM testing is the standard for rapid diagnosis, with commercial enzyme immunoassay (EIA) kits commonly used. IgM antibodies are typically detectable 4–30 days after illness onset but may not appear before day 5 of rash onset. If IgM is negative in specimens collected before day 5, repeat testing is recommended. IgG testing can confirm infection by detecting a significant rise in specific IgG levels between acute and convalescent serum samples. Rubella IgG is usually detectable by day 8 after rash onset. IgG avidity testing can distinguish recent primary infections (low avidity) from past infections or reinfections (high avidity). Molecular surveillance, including RT-PCR and genotyping, is recommended to track rubella virus epidemiology and document the elimination of endemic transmission. Genotyping can differentiate wild-type rubella virus from vaccine strains. Infants with CRS should be considered infectious until two negative cultures of clinical specimens, obtained one month apart after three months of age, confirm the absence of rubella virus. Effective communication strategies are essential for introducing rubella vaccines into national immunization programs. These strategies should include advocacy, social mobilization, and media engagement to promote vaccine acceptance and address public concerns about vaccine safety.
